methodological_rigor.justification: This is a prospective, multicenter (10 US sites), cooperative group (SWOG) phase 2 single-arm trial with a pre-specified primary endpoint (pCR rate), formal sample size calculation (n=25 with 90% power), and a one-sided exact binomial test against a specified null hypothesis (5% pCR). Central pathology review was a pre-planned exploratory endpoint providing concordance validation. Competing risks analysis for melanoma-specific survival and reverse Kaplan-Meier for median follow-up estimation reflect statistical sophistication appropriate for the design.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Neoadjuvant pembrolizumab achieving 71% pCR in desmoplastic melanoma is directly practice-relevant for a rare cancer where surgical morbidity is substantial and repeat procedures are common. The 3-year RFS of 74% and OS of 87% with no melanoma-attributed deaths support the therapeutic value. Findings may reduce surgical scope and morbidity, and the data inform cooperative group trial design for this understudied subtype.

reporting_quality.justification: The CONSORT diagram is provided and the study follows Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary standards. Primary endpoint, null hypothesis, power calculation, and significance threshold are explicitly stated. Source data for figures are available. The central pathology review protocol is pre-specified in the supplementary information. Minor gap: while pCR as a surrogate for OS is acknowledged as a limitation, the validation evidence linking pCR to OS in desmoplastic melanoma specifically is limited.

novelty_literature.justification: This is the first prospective cooperative group clinical trial of neoadjuvant anti-PD-1 in desmoplastic melanoma specifically, validating the retrospective observation of high response rates in this subtype. The 71% pCR rate substantially exceeds rates in other melanoma subtypes and combination regimens, directly filling a documented gap in evidence for this rare entity. Serial biopsy analysis adds mechanistic insight into response kinetics.

writing_presentation.justification: Well-organized with clear endpoint definitions, patient flow diagrams, and informative survival plots. The discussion is appropriately self-critical about pCR as a primary endpoint and the limitations of a single-arm design. Genomic analysis is contextually integrated. Minor issue: the article text occasionally repeats the same clinical response statistics across sections, and the redacted adjuvant therapy text creates a gap in the discussion.

key_strengths: 71% pCR rate with prospective pre-specified design statistically ruling out the null hypothesis, providing robust evidence for a rare melanoma subtype
Multicenter US cooperative group design with 10 sites, central pathology concordance validation, and 3-year follow-up demonstrating 87% OS
Genomic characterization (WES) confirming ultra-high TMB and NF1/TP53/CDKN2A driver landscape consistent with UV-mediated desmoplastic biology
Serial biopsies capturing on-therapy response kinetics provide translational mechanistic support
None of the 28 patients died from melanoma, supporting exceptional long-term disease control
key_concerns: Single-arm design without randomized control arm limits causal inference; pCR as surrogate for OS has not been formally validated in desmoplastic melanoma specifically
Small sample size (n=28) and rare disease restrict subgroup analyses; WES available in only 16 patients limits genomic conclusions
Exclusively white (96%) and elderly (median 75 years) cohort limits generalizability to other demographic groups
Adjuvant pembrolizumab was not received by any patient despite being allowed per protocol, creating a confound in interpreting long-term survival
chief_reviewer.rationale: A landmark prospective cooperative group study in a rare and understudied melanoma subtype with exceptional response rates and favorable long-term outcomes; the rigor of the cooperative group design, pre-specified endpoint, and central pathology review justify tier 2 placement despite the inherent limitations of a single-arm rare-disease trial.
